# Recipe: UX asset handoff (approved mockups → build-ready assets)

**Use when:** a bmad-ux package is approved and epics/build are next, or a handoff is incomplete. The `pf-ux-asset-handoff` skill carries the phase order and the hard rules; this recipe carries the detail. The mechanical steps are `Tools/pf/ux-handoff.py` (run `--help`).

**Gate.** `python3 Tools/pf/ux-handoff.py check --ws <ws>` exits `0` (warnings are reported, not
hidden). `python3 Tools/pf/ux-handoff.py manifest --ws <ws> --check` exits `0` after any
re-extraction, and in a 3D game `python3 Tools/pf/ux-handoff.py models --ws <ws> --check` exits `0`
too. The handoff writes planning artifacts only, so there is no Unity gate here. The import story
that consumes ASSET-MAP.md later proves PPU 1 with `Framework/Doctor` (check 14 names a missing
`SpriteImportDefaults.cs`), and its `finish` stories run `Tools/pf/visual-judge.sh` against the
SURFACES.md captures.

## Part A — Extraction: approved mockup → reusable sprites

Approved mockups are flattened PNGs. There are no layers to export, so each reusable object is
**re-painted from the mockup by an image model** and then checked by eye against its source. The
result is a restored raster master, not a lossless export, and the provenance says so.

The door is the framework's `Tools/pf/asset-gen.py` (Codex image_gen, headless, read-only). Read
the `pf-asset-gen` skill once for its request fields, exit codes and the rule that a
selected PNG is committed source nobody regenerates.

### 1. The job list — `<ws>/ui-kit/sprite-jobs.json`

One JSON array. Split it across `sprite-jobs-*.json` files if it grows; the scripts read them all.

```json
[
  {"id": "card-frame", "ref": "03-gameplay.png", "kind": "sprite", "region": [412, 506, 560, 636],
   "subject": "the plain cream rounded card frame. Remove the picture, chain link and markers. Keep the thick dark brown contour and golden lower bevel.",
   "aspect": "168:148", "slice": [0.18, 0.18, 0.18, 0.18]},
  {"id": "bg-map-jungle", "ref": "02-map.png", "kind": "plate",
   "subject": "the jungle map scenery: path, ground, foliage and sky."}
]
```

| Field | Rule |
|---|---|
| `id` | Lowercase kebab, stable forever. Group by prefix: `button-*`, `panel-*`, `icon-*`, `picture-*`, `hero-*`, `bg-*`. It becomes the file name, the manifest key and the id that stories cite. |
| `ref` | A file in `<ws>/mockups/` that the surface ledger marks approved. Pick the mockup where the object is largest and least covered. |
| `kind` | `sprite` has transparent pixels. `plate` is an opaque full-frame background. |
| `region` | Sprites only: `[x0, y0, x1, y1]` in **mockup pixels**, tight around the object. Measure it on the PNG (Pillow, or read the image and estimate, then check with a crop). The script pads it by 8%. |
| `subject` | What to keep and what to remove, in the words of DESIGN.md. Name everything that overlaps the object (text, counters, a neighbouring card) so the model removes it. |
| `aspect` | Optional. Source aspect ratio when it matters, like a card or button footprint. |
| `slice` | Optional. Suggested 9-slice fractions L, T, R, B for quiet materials (panels, buttons, capsules, ribbons). Leave it out for illustrations and icons. |

#### What earns a job

- **One reusable object per job.** A button material, one icon, one card frame, one chain link, one
  picture. A composite illustration that only ever appears whole (a win-card fan, a hero scene) is one
  job of its own.
- **Materials separate from content.** The card frame and the object picture are two sprites, and so
  are the button body and its icon.
- **No text, ever.** Words, digits, prices, level numbers and stock counts are live text rendered
  through `LocKey`. Pictograms such as a check mark or a question mark are fine.
- **States are overlays, not sprites,** unless the mockup shows a genuinely different material (for
  example a selected tab that is a different plank). Pressed, disabled and focus stay code-side.
- Walk DESIGN.md §Components, EXPERIENCE.md §Component Patterns and **every approved mockup**. An
  object you can see in a mockup that no component names is a finding. Log it and ask; never invent
  a component to house it.
- **Curved stretchable materials are cut in pieces.** An arched ribbon or a banner with shaped
  tails cannot 9-slice without flattening. Extract it as `<id>-tail-l`, `<id>-center`, `<id>-tail-r`
  when localized text must widen it.
- **Want a small-size export too?** Record it as a variant in the asset map (for example a 256 px
  picture for thumbnails). It is not a second job.
- Native OS and Editor chrome (store sheets, consent dialogs, Unity Editor panels) are not game
  sprites.

**Checkpoint.** Show the user the list before any generation: counts per group, the mockup each
comes from, and the estimated cost (jobs × variants × ~60 s, run 3–4 at a time). Generation spends
real quota, so it waits for an explicit go.

### 2. Requests

```sh
python3 Tools/pf/ux-handoff.py requests --ws <ws>            # all jobs
python3 Tools/pf/ux-handoff.py requests --ws <ws> --ids a,b  # a subset
```

- `sprite` becomes `mode: generate`. Image 1 is a padded, upscaled crop of `region` (what to
  reproduce) and Image 2 is the whole mockup (style only). It returns an isolated sprite, usually at
  1254×1254 whatever size you ask for. That is fine: the asset map sets the import size.
- `plate` becomes `mode: edit` on the whole mockup, with the UI painted out. It keeps the mockup's
  size.
- Requests land in `Tools/AssetGen/requests/ux-<id>.json`, and `out` points at
  `<ws>/ui-kit/assets/sprites/<id>.png`. Review a few requests before running them all; the prompt is
  the lever.

### 3. Run, look, select

```sh
python3 Tools/pf/asset-gen.py run Tools/AssetGen/requests/ux-<id>.json --variants 2   # unsandboxed: needs network
python3 Tools/pf/ux-handoff.py sheet --ws <ws> --beside-crop  # after selecting
python3 Tools/pf/asset-gen.py select Tools/AssetGen/requests/ux-<id>.json <n>
```

- **Choose by looking**, never by the first exit 0. Put the candidates beside the source crop at
  display size. Reject any candidate that changed the design, such as a different rim, palette or
  proportion, or added detail. Reject any that simplified toward flat or vector art, left text in,
  or clipped the silhouette.
- One vision call over a small JPEG contact sheet catches a gross mismatch. It flips on subtle ones,
  so trust its verdict only when two runs agree.
- `select` writes `<png>.gen.json` with `status: pending-user-review`. A person flips the status when
  they approve the batch; the contact sheets are what they look at.
- **Budget:** at most ~6 generations per asset. If two rounds miss, the request is the problem, not
  luck. Tighten `region`, name the overlapping clutter in `subject`, or pick a mockup where the object
  is less covered. Then escalate to the user.
- Run in batches of 3–4 in parallel. A timed-out call may still be running; never re-issue it blindly.

#### No transparency?

`ux-handoff.py manifest` lists sprites without transparent pixels under `noAlpha`. Re-issue those
with `ux-handoff.py requests --ids <id> --keyed --force`, which asks for a flat `#FF00FF` ground. Then:

```sh
python3 Tools/pf/ux-handoff.py key-out <ws>/ui-kit/assets/sprites/<id>.png
```

Look at the result on the checkerboard sheet: magenta fringes mean `--tol`/`--soft` need raising.

#### Plates

An edit keeps the mockup's size, and generated mockups are often **smaller than the reference
canvas** (941×1672 against 1080×1920). Covering the screen is then an upscale, more so with bleed on
tall phones. Flag this in the asset map's open items. The fix is a higher-resolution repaint (a
`generate` request with the plate as reference, then a person checks it), never a silent resize.

A plate with its UI painted out is **not** proven seamless. When a plate must tile (a scrolling map),
stack three copies vertically and look at the joins. Record the result in the asset map's open items.
The build stage owns seam acceptance.

### 4. Manifest

```sh
python3 Tools/pf/ux-handoff.py manifest --ws <ws>
```

Writes `<ws>/ui-kit/sprite-manifest.json`: size, alpha bounds, visible bounds, hashes, source
mockup, provenance status, draw mode and slice suggestion per sprite, plus `missing` and `noAlpha`.
Re-run it after every re-extraction; `--check` exits 1 when it is stale.

If the package already has a manifest from an earlier run in another format, do not overwrite it.
The checker reads any manifest with `assets[].{id,file,kind,sha256,visibleBoundsXYXY}`.

## Part B — ASSET-MAP.md: which sprite, what size, where

The file a build agent opens when a story says "use the card frame". It is **derived**: DESIGN.md
and EXPERIENCE.md win on any conflict, and the map cites where each number came from.

### Why it exists

Restored masters come out at the model's resolution. They are typically 5–10× the on-screen size
(a 1335×1178 card-frame master for a card roughly 150 px wide) and at arbitrary aspect. The rig
reads **1 texture px = 1 canvas reference px = 1 world unit** with sprite PPU 1, so a master
imported as-is is a card 1335 units wide. The map fixes each sprite's **target size on the
reference canvas** so the import story can resize it deterministically.

### Front matter (machine-readable, read by `ux-handoff.py check`)

```yaml
---
reference_canvas: [1080, 1920]      # from the rig / capture profile
ppu: 1
source_root: ui-kit/assets/sprites  # relative to the workspace
dest_root: Assets/<Sku>/Content/UI
sprites:
  card-frame:
    source: ui-kit/assets/sprites/card-frame.png
    master: [1335, 1178]
    target: [168, 148]              # reference px == world units at PPU 1
    scale: 0.1418                   # target / master visible size
    draw: sliced                    # simple | sliced | tiled
    border_px: [30, 27, 30, 27]     # L,T,R,B at TARGET size; sliced only
    pivot: [0.5, 0.5]
    host: Renderer-WorldRoot        # uGUI-<render layer> | Renderer-WorldRoot | undecided
    dest: Assets/<Sku>/Content/UI/board/card-frame.png
    used_by: [picture-card]
    size_source: spec               # spec | mock-measured | kit-css | assumption
    size_note: "DESIGN.md §Asset production: 168×148 reference footprint"
    variants:                       # optional extra exports of the same master
      - {target: [256, 256], dest: "Assets/<Sku>/Content/UI/album/card-frame@256.png", use: thumbnail}
unmapped:                           # manifest sprites deliberately not mapped, each with a reason
  some-id: "superseded by …"
---
```

### Sizing, in order of precedence

1. **spec**: a number in DESIGN.md (geometry tables, component tokens, the asset production table).
   Later decisions supersede earlier ones, and `.memlog.md` gives the order. Cite the section.
2. **mock-measured**: measure the object on its approved mockup and scale by
   `reference_width / mock_width` (for example 1080/941 = 1.14772). Cite the mockup and the rectangle.
3. **kit-css**: a size from an HTML kit's CSS, scaled by the kit's preview factor (a 360×640 preview
   is ×3). This is secondary evidence only.
4. **assumption**: tag it `[ASSUMPTION]` in the table too. It shows up as a checker warning and in
   the report.

Declare the crop once at the top of the front matter (`crop: visibleBoundsXYXY`,
`padding_px: 2`) and the mock scale (`mock_to_reference: 1.14772`), so the import story resizes
the crop and not the whole master.

When a spec token and the approved mockup disagree (a 168 token against a 192 band the mock
matches), use the value the current geometry needs, cite both in `size_note`, and list it for the
DESIGN.md owner. Never quietly pick one.

Keep the target aspect equal to the master's **visible-bounds** aspect (alpha ≥ 32) unless the spec
says otherwise, and say so when the import must crop to visible bounds first. A target larger than
the master's visible size means upscaling: flag it, since the master may be too low-resolution.

### Draw mode

- `sliced`: only quiet materials whose centre and edges can stretch, such as panels, buttons,
  capsules, ribbon centres and progress tracks. Convert the manifest's slice fractions to pixels **at
  target size**, and check that the corners keep their silhouette.
- `simple`: illustrations, icons, pictures, hardware and anything with detail in the middle. Never
  stretch these.
- `tiled`: repeating plates (a scrolling map ground). Seam acceptance is an open item until someone
  looks at three stacked copies.

### Host (AGENTS.md rule 16: parent per object)

Ask what the object anchors to first.

- **Screen edge** (HUD, top bar, tabs, toasts): `uGUI-Ui`. Dialog content: `uGUI-Popup`. System
  overlays: `uGUI-Overlay`. A uGUI marker that follows a world point but draws over gameplay and under
  the HUD (a waiting clock, a payout bubble, an emote) is `uGUI-OverlayGamePlay`; `uGUI-GamePlay` and
  `uGUI-UnderGamePlay` name the other two framework layers.
- **The world** (board, cards, hooks, chains, world ground): then ask how it draws. A `Renderer`
  goes to `Renderer-WorldRoot`; a world canvas goes to `uGUI-<layer>` via `GetHost(id)`.
- If DESIGN.md or EXPERIENCE.md does not decide it, write `undecided` and list it under open items.
  Never guess a spine decision into the map.

Background plates sized to the screen are full-bleed: target covers the reference canvas plus
bleed. At runtime they size from `IWorldViewport`; never hard-code a camera size.

### Destination

Everything lands under `Assets/<Sku>/…`, which is where `SpriteImportDefaults` applies PPU 1 on first
import. Group by component family (`Content/UI/hud/`, `Content/UI/board/`, `Content/UI/dialog/`, …).
The masters stay in the design package, outside `Assets/`. The import step resizes them (Lanczos,
alpha kept, ~2 px transparent padding against atlas fringes) and writes the runtime PNG. That step
belongs to the first build story, not to this skill.

### Body

1. A short header: purpose, authority, the import pipeline above, and that stories cite sprite ids
   from this file.
2. A table per component group: component → sprite ids → target → draw → host → dest.
3. Sprites no component uses (content pictures, album art, plates) and how each is treated. Content
   pictures take the card picture-slot size.
4. **Open items**: assumptions, undecided hosts, unsuitable 9-slices, upscales, seam checks, and ids
   that the component manifest and the sprite manifest disagree on.

## Part C — Wiring the handoff into the design docs

Downstream skills read the **spines**. `bmad-create-epics-and-stories` extracts requirements from
DESIGN.md and EXPERIENCE.md, and `bmad-build` transcribes a story's Visual Contract from the sources
its intent names. A file the spines do not point at, with a sentence saying what it is for, does not
exist for them. A file they point at without that sentence gets misread. The failure this skill was
born from: an HTML kit's composed screens were linked as a "production reference", drifted from the
approved mockups, and were about to become the layout agents built from.

### 1. The reference paragraph

Put the same paragraph at the top of **DESIGN.md §Brand & Style** and **EXPERIENCE.md §Foundation**.
Replace any older "production reference" line; never add a second one.

```markdown
Production references: the [approved mockups](mockup-index.html) define layout, composition and
finish, one PNG per surface in [SURFACES.md](SURFACES.md), with the deliberate mock-versus-product
differences in [DIVERGENCES.md](DIVERGENCES.md). The [sprite set](ui-kit/sprite-manifest.json) is
the source of **sprite assets and component states only**; which sprite each component uses, and
its import size, is in [ASSET-MAP.md](ASSET-MAP.md). These spines stay authoritative over every one
of them.
```

In a 3D game, add one sentence to the same paragraph: *The [model inventory](models/model-manifest.json)
lists every 3D model and animation clip with its file and measured facts; which model each actor
uses, its import scale and the state that plays each clip are in ASSET-MAP.md.* The checker fails
a 3D package whose spines link neither the model manifest nor MODELS.md.

- If there is no `mockup-index.html`, link the `mockups/` folder or SURFACES.md instead.
- If the package has an HTML component kit, link it as the sprite and state source. If it also has
  **composed screens**, add one sentence saying they are not a visual reference and that builds
  follow the mockups.

### 2. The handoff's asset table

If the package has an asset handoff document (`UI-ASSET-HANDOFF.md` or similar), its package table
must name **the sprite ids actually delivered**, not proposed stems. An agent that reads
`ui-button-{variant}` goes looking for a file that does not exist. Use this shape:

| Package | Delivered sprite ids | Component behavior and states | Gap |
|---|---|---|---|

A 3D game adds the same table for models: `| Actor | Model id | Clips (id → state) | Gap |`. A clip
the motion spec calls for that no file holds is a Gap with the animation owner's name on it.

**Gap** names art the design calls for that no sprite covers yet, such as markers, badges or
endcaps. A gap is produced later from the approved style (`pf-asset-gen`), never by redrawing
approved art. The checker does not parse this table. Instead, verify coverage with a quick script:
every manifest id appears once, and every id in the table exists.

### 3. Surface ledger

`SURFACES.md` and `DIVERGENCES.md` follow `.claude/skills/bmad-ux/references/finish-handoff.md`
exactly. Where a SKU's bmad-ux lacks that reference, the minimum `ux-handoff.py check` reads is:
SURFACES.md front matter `capture_profile`, `capture: {width, height}` and `surfaces:` keyed by a
surface slug, each with `version`, `approved`, `approved_by`, `capture` (a PNG path, or `none` plus
`reason`), optional `states: [{name, capture}]`, `elements` (dotted ids of components the spines
define) and `excludes` (elements owned by other surfaces). DIVERGENCES.md has one heading per
captured surface containing its key, with a `Mock does | Product does | Why | Do not report` table
or an explicit "None".

Differences when the package predates that reference:

- **Keep the existing mockup filenames.** Renaming to `key-{surface}-{NN}` breaks every link in the
  spines and the gallery for no gain. Record `version: '01'` and cite the real file.
- **Record the size rule.** Generated mockups are rarely at the capture profile, for example
  941×1672 against 1080×1920. Write in the front matter how the build capture and the mock are
  compared: scale to a common size, state the aspect difference, and say that the size difference
  must not be reported.
- **Name duplicates and states.** A byte-identical second mockup becomes `duplicate_of`. Theme
  variants of one surface become `states:` with their own captures.
- **Mock-versus-spine conflicts.** When a mockup shows something the spines forbid or never define,
  such as a wrong button colour, an undefined plaque or a feature the gates block, handle it by
  type. Where the spine is explicit, declare it in DIVERGENCES.md ("Spine precedence") so a referee
  does not demand the mock's version. Where the spine is silent, **do not declare it**: log it as an
  `assumption` open item and put it in the report for a DESIGN or EXPERIENCE owner to decide.
- A plate that only teaches (several states in one image) cannot be reproduced by one runtime frame.
  Record it as `capture: none`, and map each panel to the runtime state a finish story captures
  instead.
- A mockup that shows a native Editor or OS surface is a layout reference, not finish-judged. Say so,
  with the reason.

### 4. Finish bar

`DESIGN.md §Do's and Don'ts` ends with `### Finish bar` (shape in finish-handoff.md). **Elicit it;
do not author it.** The best source is the user's own rejections during the UX run, logged in
`.memlog.md`: "too small", "coarse", "looks slapped together", "replace the SVG art". Quote their
direction, and make every line judgeable from one screenshot. When you draft it from the memlog, log
an `assumption` entry and ask the user to confirm the wording in your final report. When the memlog
has no rejections, ask the user before writing it.

### 5. Memlog

Log every change to the package through the bmad script, never by hand:

```sh
uv run _bmad/scripts/memlog.py append --workspace <ws> --type change --text "<what changed + why>"
```

Use `change` for edits, `assumption` for drafted wording or sizes awaiting confirmation, and
`decision` only for something the user decided.

## Part D — 3D models and animation clips

Only when the game's world is drawn with 3D models. The checker decides that the same way the skill
does: `models/*/model.gen.json`, a `MODELS.md`, or an FBX/glTF anywhere in the package (outside
`.working/`). The last case with no inventory is a failure, so a supplied FBX cannot ride along
unmapped.

The models themselves come from `pf-model-gen` (or an artist, or the SKU's own pipeline), and the
clips from whoever owns animation. This part never makes either one. It records what exists,
measures it, and says how the build imports it.

### 1. The inventory — `<ws>/models/model-sources.json` → `model-manifest.json`

`pf-model-gen` outputs are found on their own: each `models/<id>/model.gen.json` becomes a model
with its FBX, its moving parts (from the request) and its provenance status.
Everything else is declared, as one JSON array:

```json
[
  {"id": "crew-washer", "mesh": "animations/crew-washer/crew-washer-animated.fbx", "rig": "skinned",
   "status": "approved",
   "clips": [{"id": "idle", "loop": true, "seconds": 2.0},
             {"id": "celebrate", "loop": false, "seconds": 1.2}]},
  {"id": "vehicle-sedan", "mesh": "animations/vehicle-sedan/vehicle-sedan-animated.fbx",
   "anim": "animations/vehicle-sedan/vehicle-sedan-animated.glb", "rig": "transform",
   "clips": [{"id": "queue_drive", "loop": true, "seconds": 2.0},
             {"id": "brake", "file": "animations/vehicle-sedan/clips/brake.fbx", "loop": false}]}
]
```

| Field | Rule |
|---|---|
| `id` | Kebab, stable forever: the id stories cite. Reusing a `pf-model-gen` id **merges**: the declared fields win, the model-gen provenance is still checked. |
| `mesh` | Workspace-relative FBX/glTF the build imports. For a rigged or animated version of a model-gen model, point at that file. |
| `anim` | Optional. The file holding the takes when it is not the mesh (a combined glTF, say). |
| `rig` | `none` (static, or parts moved only in code) · `transform` (takes move whole objects) · `skinned` (an armature). |
| `clips` | Per clip: `id` (the take's name in the file), optional `file` (a per-clip FBX; a file named after the clip may hold one take of any name), `loop` (required: the import sets it), `seconds` (the length the spines give it). |
| `status` | Optional provenance for a supplied file: `approved` when a person approved it, else it reads `unknown-provenance`. |
| `parts` | Optional. Moving parts that must exist by name. Model-gen models take them from their request. |

```sh
python3 Tools/pf/ux-handoff.py models --ws <ws> --probe   # writes models/model-manifest.json
python3 Tools/pf/ux-handoff.py models --ws <ws> --check   # 1 when a file or the declaration moved
```

The manifest records, per file, its hash and its **facts**: size in metres, triangles, named
transforms (objects and bones), bone count and every take with its length. Facts come from
model.gen.json for an untouched model-gen FBX, from a glTF's own JSON (no Blender needed), or, with
`--probe`, from one headless Blender run over every FBX that has none yet. Facts of an unchanged file
are reused, so the probe is paid once per file. Without facts a clip is reported **unverified**, not
passed. Triangle counts are recorded for later optimization and never gated by the handoff.

What the checker then fails:

- a file whose hash moved since the manifest, or a model-gen FBX that no longer matches its
  model.gen.json (it was hand-edited: rebuild through `model-gen.py rebuild`);
- a `skinned` rig with no bones; clips on a `rig: none` model; a moving
  part that is neither an object nor a bone in the file;
- a declared clip whose take is not in its file, a clip with no `loop`, and a clip whose measured
  length differs from the declared `seconds` by more than 5%. That last one is usually a frame-rate
  mismatch at export (keys authored at 30 fps written into a 24 fps file play 25% slow in Unity).
  Report it to the file's owner. Never "fix" it by editing the declared length.

### 2. ASSET-MAP.md — the `models:` block

```yaml
model_import_scale: 100             # world units per metre, applied ONCE at import; or `undecided`
models:
  vehicle-sedan:
    dest: Assets/<Sku>/Content/Models/vehicles/vehicle-sedan.fbx
    host: Renderer-WorldRoot        # Renderer-WorldRoot | undecided
    used_by: [vehicle-actor]
    rig: transform                  # must match the manifest
    animation: clips+code           # none | clips | code | clips+code
    clips:
      queue_drive: {used_by: "Queued state, loops while the queue advances"}
      brake:       {used_by: "Arrived event"}
    unmapped_clips:
      wash_surfaces: "replaced by the shader-driven surface states"
    code_parts: [Wheel_FL, Wheel_FR] # transforms a View moves itself
unmapped_models:
  module-curb-corner: "baked into the map scene; not imported on its own"
```

- **One scale.** Models are authored in metres and the rig is 1 px = 1 world unit, so a metre
  becomes `model_import_scale` units **exactly once**, at import. Where the 3D world sits on the rig
  is an architecture decision: until `bmad-architecture` makes it, write `undecided` (a warning). A
  per-model `import_scale` that differs needs a `scale_note` saying why, or the checker fails it as a
  scale applied twice.
- **Host.** A mesh draws through a Renderer, so rule 16 leaves `Renderer-WorldRoot` or
  `undecided`. A 3D picture inside a dialog is a render-to-texture decision for architecture, not a
  uGUI host.
- **Destination.** Under `Assets/<Sku>/…`, grouped by family (`Content/Models/vehicles/`, `…/crew/`,
  `…/props/`). Prefer FBX; a glTF destination warns, because Unity needs an importer package for it.
- **Every clip is accounted for.** With `animation` naming clips, each manifest clip of the model is
  mapped with the state or event that plays it, or listed under `unmapped_clips` with a reason.
  `code_parts` must be transforms that exist in the file.
- Every manifest model is mapped or listed under `unmapped_models` with a reason (map-scene pieces,
  superseded drafts).

Open items in the body: an undecided scale or host, files without facts, clips whose length is off,
and models still `pending-user-review`.
